title: Pi (Disrupt SF 2017 final)

transcript.text: Please take it away. All right. Thanks Anthony Two days ago. We unveiled the world's first contactless wireless charger on this stage And we can't wait to show it to all of you live This is how we charge right now We live in a tangled nest of wires We're constantly replacing ones that break or get lost and worst of all if we forget to plug in our phones Die at the worst possible moment Charging is a terrible experience.

Thankfully, last Tuesday, a famous smartphone maker came with the solution, a new charging technology, the charging pad. I think we've all seen this before. The year was 2009 and the company was Palm. After all these years, it's still a pad. You can't use your phone while it's charging, it's kind of ugly and worst of all each section of pad can only charge one device at a time.

So if you've got a lot of devices you're gonna need a ton of pads everywhere or a ginormous one to do them all. Pads are not the solution. So how do we get truly wireless charging? Well three years ago I asked the same question. I was a doctor working at the MIT Media Lab looking for a new way to to power medical devices. And that's when I met Li Xin, a gold medalist at China's famous Tsinghua University and a PhD student in MIT's computer science and AI lab.

And he had a breakthrough. An historic mathematical proof that unlocked the solution to wireless power by the bending of magnetic fields. Introducing Pi, the world's first contactless wireless charging device. Let's go to the demo, please. Could we have the camera onto the demo table, please? Wonderful. Thank you. So this is Pi. To use it, simply take a device, bring it nearby, and look, it's charging. And Leishan can even continue to use the device and move it around in different directions.

And then we can add a second device. And there we go. It's charging, too. can add a third and a fourth and it's not just for iPhone either. We're going to have an Android device out here. There it is. It's charging. Now let's try something even harder, something that needs more power. How about an iPad? And look, there, it's charging too. We've got five devices now charging simultaneously at different angles from just one pi.

Back to the PowerPoint, please. Thank you. Now in the demo that you just saw, you'll notice that the cases have, the phones have cases on them and to be clear, when the iPhone 8 and X start arriving you will not need a case to use Pi. Similar for upcoming Android phones supporting the Qi standard. We built these cases to enable people with popular legacy devices to be able to charge as well as to charge your tablets which don't have magnetic receivers.

Now over the years, a number of other companies have promised wireless power. They've tried microwaves, ultrasound, lasers. None of these technologies are safe at power levels needed to charge a phone. You wouldn't be willing to live inside a microwave just to charge your iPhone, would you? Well, the FCC agrees and has blocked them. Instead, we built Pi around a safe magnetic charging standard. But until today, magnetic charging was very limited.

You had to put a device down perfectly parallel to the receiver to get any power. But thanks to our incredible team and Leishan's breakthrough, our patented platform can power multiple devices at any angle. It's safe, it's affordable, and it's FCC compliant. Our business model has two parts. First, we will sell Pi directly to consumers. We have over 50% gross margins and anticipate a very high lifetime value per customer.

If you like pie in your kitchen, you're going to want one in the living room, the bedroom, and in the office and enterprise. Second, we are opening the pie platform for use by existing consumer electronics OEMs. We're already in discussions with several of them. More on that in a second. We are backed by some incredible investors, Jeff Clavier from Soft Tech, Hadley Harris from ENIAC, and Next View Ventures, Lee Hauer.

We're so thankful for all their mentorship through this process. We want to thank this TechCrunch audience because we've had some incredible results since we launched. We have had outreach from 10 of the world's top consumer electronics brands, over 50 publications worldwide have written about pie and over 8,500 of you have reserved your pies. So as a special thank you we are offering anyone who reserves a pie in the next hour a $31.41 discount when pie starts shipping.

To reserve go to piecharging.com now and soon you'll experience how pie makes everyday magic. Thank you. Wait, did you bring any extra cases? Because I'm at 7%. Pardon me? I'm at 7%. Do you have any extra cases?

brief.headline: Dig deeper: the core 'contactless charging at a distance' claim is unverified and live drift shows current devices need special cases, while the competitive framing is contradicted by existing multi-device pads.
brief.summary: Pi claims to be the first contactless wireless charger. It says it charges five devices (iPhone, Android, iPad) at different angles from one unit while they move. It plans to sell direct to consumers at over 50% gross margin and to license the platform to OEMs, and it cites over 8,500 reservations. Palm's 2009 charging pad and the competitors' microwave, ultrasound and laser attempts check out. The claim that each pad section charges only one device is contradicted: free-positioning pads from Aira and Belkin charge several devices on one surface. The central product claim is unverified, and drift weakens it: the demo relied on cases, tablets have no magnetic receivers, and 'discussions with several OEMs' became 'outreach from 10'. FCC compliance, safety and margin claims were stated without any support.
strengths: Live multi-device demo (five devices, including an Android phone and an iPad) is a concrete, testable product claim
Competitor landscape is accurate: Palm's 2009 pad and the microwave, ultrasound and laser attempts were confirmed
Two revenue paths (direct sale and OEM licensing), with a claimed 50%+ gross margin and 8,500+ reservations as early demand signal
Named seed investors (SoftTech, ENIAC, NextView) and a technical team with MIT ties, though none of this is checked yet

red_flags.text: Core claim of charging at a distance with no contact is unverified. The founder later admitted the demo devices were in cases, built for legacy phones and tablets without magnetic receivers. This suggests a case or receiver accessory is needed today, which undercuts 'contactless' and the 'just bring it nearby' framing, and the iPad result in particular.

Differentiation is overstated. The claim that each pad section charges one device is contradicted by free-positioning pads (Aira FreePower, Belkin TrueFreedom) that charge several devices anywhere on a surface. The pitch never says what Pi does that those can't.

Regulatory and safety claims are asserted without evidence. Pi is called FCC compliant and safe, and the FCC is said to have 'blocked' microwave, ultrasound and laser charging. None of this is checked, and no authorization or test data was offered.

OEM traction is softer than first stated. 'Already in discussions with several' became 'outreach from 10', which is inbound interest. The licensing model, and the reservations (unverified, reservations rather than paid orders), rest on this.

Unverified claims about the technology and team: a 'patented' platform, the mathematical proof behind it, and an inconsistent co-founder name (Li Xin vs Leishan, possibly a transcription error). The 50%+ gross margin is stated before the product ships.

questions: Can we run Pi on our own devices, with no cases, and what are the real charging distance, watts delivered per device and efficiency with five devices charging?
Which devices charge today without a case, and what do the cases contain (receiver coil, magnets)? How does that differ from existing Qi pads?
What can Pi do that Aira FreePower, Belkin TrueFreedom or ZENS Liberty can't, and what patents protect it?
What FCC authorization do you hold today (FCC ID), and what exposure testing covers multi-device charging?
Of the 10 OEM contacts, how many are in active talks, and has any signed an NDA, pilot or LOI? Are the 8,500 reservations paid or refundable, and what is the unit cost behind the 50%+ margin?
evidence_requests: FCC equipment authorization grant or test lab reports with the FCC ID, plus RF exposure and safety results
Third-party lab report on power vs. distance and angle, efficiency and thermals with five devices
Head-to-head comparison against free-positioning pads, plus a bill of materials and unit cost sheet backing the 50%+ gross margin
Reservation data (paid vs. unpaid, deposits) and evidence of OEM contacts (emails, NDAs, LOIs)
live_notes: Earlier the demo implied devices charge simply by being brought near; later the founder said the phones had cases, built for legacy devices, and that the iPad needed one because tablets lack magnetic receivers.
Co-founder was first named Li Xin, then Leishan (possibly a transcription error).
'Discussions with several' OEMs was later described as 'outreach from 10' top brands, which is inbound interest.

Claims made only live include 50%+ gross margin, 8,500+ reservations, FCC compliance, a patented platform, the claim that the FCC has blocked competing technologies, and case-free use with the iPhone 8/X and Qi Android phones.
The pitch ended with someone saying their phone was at 7% and asking for an extra case, which fits the point that cases are needed today.

outcome: Won TechCrunch Disrupt SF 2017 Startup Battlefield
